edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: Ukraine’s talks with Washington resume as an envoy heads to Moscow; Sudan’s reported toll rises above 300. In the UK and Denmark, new decisions and investigations put public policy under scrutiny.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting. Continuing coverage is included where the gather brings a meaningful update; unchanged stories from the previous edition are not repeated.

content.headline: Zelensky says US intelligence warnings are working again after Oslo talks
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky says US warnings are working again
content.standfirst: The Ukrainian president says early warnings of Russian missile attacks have resumed after talks with a Trump envoy. Steve Witkoff is due to take proposals from Oslo to a meeting with Vladimir Putin.

image.caption: Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and US envoy Steve Witkoff at the Oslo talks.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
Norge og Finland: Konstruktive samtaler om Ukraine
Ukraine war briefing: US envoy Witkoff to meet Putin after ‘constructive’ talks with Zelenskyy in Norway

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky said US intelligence sharing on Russian missile attacks “works now” after talks in Oslo with President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukraine had accused Washington of withholding intelligence, a charge US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected. Zelensky said renewed early warnings help protect civilians.

segments.title: A further test in Moscow
segments.body: Witkoff is due to meet Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday with proposals discussed in Oslo. Participants described progress, but gave few details; Putin has not publicly responded. Zelensky said Ukraine must be part of any discussions about its future. He also raised Starlink restrictions and Patriot missiles, issues whose status remains unclear.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Zelensky offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries if the US provided Patriot interceptors, and says the Pentagon had blocked transfers of missiles paid for by other countries.

content.headline: More than 300 reportedly killed in Sudan drone strikes on mourners and markets
content.shortHeadline: Sudan drone strikes reportedly kill more than 300
content.standfirst: Reports describe attacks in West Kordofan and the disputed Abyei region, including a funeral convoy and a market. Responsibility and some casualty figures remain unconfirmed.

image.caption: People wounded in the market strike are being treated at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei.

sources.originalTitle: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say

segments.body: Sources told the Sudan War Observatory that 150 people were killed in strikes in West Kordofan on Sunday, including mourners travelling to a funeral. In Abyei, a regional information minister said 153 people died when a drone struck a market on Monday. The figures have not been independently established in full.

segments.title: Responsibility remains contested
segments.body: A Sudanese military source told the BBC that the army carried out the Abyei strike, describing the market as a fuel supply site for the Rapid Support Forces. Sudan’s army has not responded to the specific allegations about these attacks, but says it does not target civilians. South Sudan has summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest the Abyei strike, amid concern the conflict could spill across the border.

segments.title: A worsening civilian crisis
segments.body: The UN says drone strikes are killing civilians and disrupting essential services as 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risk rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. The war has displaced more than 14 million people, according to the report.

content.headline: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak reaches more African countries
content.shortHeadline: Nigeria confirms Ebola case amid regional spread
content.standfirst: Nigeria says a woman who travelled from Uganda tested positive and that 44 contacts are being traced. Kenya has confirmed nine cases; the infection’s source and the Nigerian patient’s travel timeline remain unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

segments.body: Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in Abuja after a woman who had travelled from Uganda tested positive. The health ministry says it is tracing 44 contacts. Nigeria has not disclosed the woman’s nationality or when she arrived. Uganda says she had transited through the country after a business trip to eastern Congo, and that her place of infection is unknown.

segments.title: Neighbouring countries on alert
segments.body: Kenya has reported nine cases, while the outbreak has also prompted heightened surveillance elsewhere in the region. The Africa CDC’s director general called the situation an “extremely serious threat” and said it had become the most geographically extensive Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak recorded. The strain has no approved vaccine or treatment, though trials are under way.

perspectives.body: The BBC reports that all nine confirmed Kenyan cases are linked to the first patient, and that 134 of 135 listed contacts remain in quarantine. Kenya’s health director general said the patients were improving, while the doctors’ union warned of gaps in border staffing and protection for health workers.

content.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines remains in critical condition after alleged car r am
content.shortHeadline: Australian MP in critical condition after alleged attack
content.standfirst: Helen Haines was struck twice by a car outside her office in Victoria, and has lost a leg, according to local media. A man charged over the incident remains in custody as police investigate.

sources.originalTitle: What we know about Australian MP hit by car in alleged deliberate attack
No bail for alleged Helen Haines attacker as police chief warns of Australia’s ‘febrile’ political environment

segments.body: Independent MP Helen Haines, 65, was hit by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on Monday. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver allegedly reversed and struck her a second time. Haines was flown to Melbourne for surgery and remains in a critical but stable condition, the Guardian reports.

segments.title: No motive established
segments.body: Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Police say they had no intelligence indicating he posed an immediate threat; the investigation continues, and no motive has been established.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that police are considering whether to bring further charges. Federal and state police leaders also cited growing abuse and intimidation of politicians, while saying they had no specific intelligence about Nugent.

segments.body: The attack has renewed concern about threats to elected representatives. Australia’s federal police say almost one person a week is charged over threats against senior office holders and their staff. Police have announced additional safety briefings for federal MPs and a new process to help monitor threats in Victoria.

content.headline: French leaders dispute who was behind weekend riots as unrest reshapes debate
content.shortHeadline: France’s leaders dispute blame for weekend riots
content.standfirst: Government figures have blamed far-left groups for violence during protests, while students and other residents reject claims that their movement was orchestrated. A parliamentary inquiry has been proposed.

image.caption: The French prime minister has blamed far-left groups for planning some of the violence.

sources.originalTitle: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots
Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder

segments.body: French officials have accused far-left groups of organising violence during Saturday’s riots, which followed weeks of student protests. The government points to intelligence reports and masked groups attacking police vehicles. The president of the National Assembly has proposed an inquiry into how the unrest was organised.

segments.title: The dispute over protest and disorder
segments.body: Student organiser Lisa Cordat called it insulting to suggest demonstrators were being directed by politicians, saying student anger came “from the ground up”. Other people interviewed by the BBC said political blame was distracting from concerns about public services. In Marseille, business leaders reported extensive damage and the city’s mayor called the response a fiasco.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s Marseille reporting records a police union’s account of being overwhelmed, and the mayor’s criticism of police deployment and tactics. The city has introduced restrictions after widespread looting and damage.

segments.body: The riots have become an immediate political issue ahead of France’s presidential election in six months. Responsibility for the violence, the police response and the causes of the protests remain contested; the reporting distinguishes peaceful demonstrations from looting and attacks.

content.headline: Indonesia’s fires spread toxic haze as hundreds of thousands report illness
content.shortHeadline: Indonesia’s fires fuel toxic haze and illness
content.standfirst: Fires have burned around 1.9 million hectares in Indonesia this year, according to a satellite platform, while the health ministry has recorded more than 277,000 respiratory cases. Smoke has reached neighbouring countries.

image.caption: Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks.

sources.originalTitle: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze

segments.body: Wildfires have burned an estimated 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, with about one million hectares thought to have burned in September alone, according to the satellite platform Nusantara Atlas. Smoke from forest, swamp and peat fires has spread across parts of Southeast Asia.

segments.title: Health and livelihoods under strain
segments.body: Indonesia’s Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections by mid-October; more than 62,000 involved children under five. Residents describe struggling to follow advice to stay indoors, while farmers, vendors and other workers face a choice between lost income and exposure to the haze.

Officials say they have deployed more than 60,000 personnel and used water bombing and weather modification to fight the fires. Researchers say peat fires can smoulder underground for months and are difficult to extinguish as drought reduces water supplies. The report links this year’s unusually harsh conditions to a strong El Niño.

content.headline: Musk says Tesla and SpaceX committees are considering a possible merger
content.shortHeadline: Tesla and SpaceX examine possible merger
content.standfirst: Elon Musk says special committees at both companies are assessing a deal, but have not agreed terms. Shareholders would have to approve any merger.

image.caption: Elon Musk leads both Tesla and SpaceX.

sources.originalTitle: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
Elon Musk åbner for mulig fusion af Tesla og SpaceX

segments.body: Elon Musk said he supports the idea of merging Tesla and SpaceX and that committees at both companies have been formed to examine it. He cautioned that no terms have been agreed and there is no guarantee a deal will happen. Musk said he is not participating in the discussions because he could have conflicts of interest.

segments.title: A potentially vast deal
segments.body: The BBC puts Tesla’s valuation at about $1.5tn and SpaceX’s at about $2tn, meaning a combination would rank among the largest mergers in history. Musk said shareholder approval would be required. SpaceX is expanding in cloud computing as well as rockets and satellite internet; the companies have also joined forces on chip manufacturing.

perspectives.body: DR reports that Musk’s comments are the clearest public confirmation so far that the companies are formally discussing a merger, while stressing that the committees have not settled its terms and shareholders would decide.

content.headline: US contact with Myanmar’s junta raises questions about a policy shift
content.shortHeadline: US engagement with Myanmar’s junta comes under scrutiny
content.standfirst: A senior US official met Myanmar’s leader, and Washington has removed some business figures from its sanctions list. Analysts say contact has increased, but substantive policy change is less clear.

image.caption: A senior US official recently met Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing.

sources.originalTitle: Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?

segments.body: US Assistant Secretary of State Michael Vance met Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing in Nay Pyi Taw in September, the most senior US official to meet him since the 2021 coup. The meeting’s stated focus was securing the release of detained US citizen Adam Castillo, though the two sides are understood to have discussed wider interests.

segments.title: Contact grows, but limits remain
segments.body: Washington has also removed some business figures from sanctions lists and did not condemn Myanmar’s recent election, while the junta has hired lobbyists in the US. But Myanmar adviser Richard Horsey of the International Crisis Group says less has changed in practice than headlines suggest: Min Aung Hlaing remains sanctioned, and sanctions relief will be harder to secure.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s reporting highlights the gap between renewed diplomatic contact and the limited practical case for US access to Myanmar’s rare earths, much of which is in contested areas and already extracted by Chinese companies.

segments.body: The policy debate also carries humanitarian stakes. The dismantling of USAID cut support to opposition groups, dissident media and refugees, the report says, while the end of Temporary Protected Status leaves thousands of Burmese people in the US at risk of return. It remains unclear whether Washington will pursue sustained engagement or what it will seek in exchange.

content.headline: Jackdaw gasfield approval expected to test Labour’s climate and energy policy
content.shortHeadline: Jackdaw gasfield decision tests Labour’s climate policy
content.standfirst: Ministers are expected to approve the North Sea project on Wednesday, after a court ruling forced its operators to resubmit climate information. The decision is set to prompt debate about energy security, jobs and emissions.

image.caption: An oil rig in the Cromarty Firth, Scotland.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling
What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?

segments.body: The Jackdaw gasfield is expected to receive environmental approval on Wednesday, according to the Guardian, after more than a year of deliberations. Shell and Equinor’s joint venture resubmitted its application after a court ruled that the climate impact of burning the gas had not been properly considered. The government says approval would not breach its promise against new North Sea licences because Jackdaw was licensed in 2022.

segments.title: What the decision may mean
segments.body: Campaigners say the field will supply only a small share of UK gas demand and undermine Labour’s climate commitments. The Guardian’s analysis says it is unlikely to lower household bills: prices are set in an international market, and Jackdaw’s output is too small to offset major supply shocks. It also notes the Committee on Climate Change’s view that the emissions impact of new fields is not straightforward.

perspectives.body: Campaign group Uplift argues Jackdaw will contribute around 2% of UK gas demand for about a decade and says the project will not halt the decline in North Sea jobs.

segments.body: The project’s supporters point to tax revenue, employment and domestic production. Industry estimates for Jackdaw and the separate Rosebank field include billions in tax and thousands of jobs, figures green groups dispute. The government’s decision on Rosebank, a larger project with substantially higher projected emissions, is expected later this year.

content.headline: Reform official questioned whether major donations would meet planned cap
content.shortHeadline: Reform official raised doubts over donations and proposed cap
content.standfirst: Undercover footage captures former policy head James Orr discussing whether two £36m donations would satisfy a proposed overseas donor limit. Reform says the donations are legal; the law has not yet passed.

image.caption: James Orr was suspended as Reform UK’s head of policy last month.

sources.originalTitle: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations

segments.body: James Orr, then Reform UK’s head of policy, discussed potential problems with major donations from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo in footage recorded by Verbatim in July, the Guardian reports. Orr said Harborne could be “more of a challenge” under a proposed £100,000 cap on overseas donations and described preparing the party’s “war chest” ahead of tighter rules.

segments.title: The legal question is unresolved
segments.body: Harborne and Delo later gave Reform £36m each. The proposed cap would apply retrospectively to donations made after March 2026, but it has not become law. Reform says both donations are legal and will not have to be repaid. Orr has previously denied wrongdoing and did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment; the police investigation concerns earlier allegations about electoral funding.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Harborne’s lawyers called Orr’s remarks private speculation, while Delo’s lawyers said he had taken extensive legal advice and would not speculate on a conversation he did not attend.

content.headline: Review calls for schools in England to treat antisemitism as distinct harm
content.shortHeadline: Schools in England urged to tackle antisemitism explicitly
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review recommends dedicated training, resources and stronger reporting procedures. Its survey found three in five Jewish students questioned had experienced antisemitism.

image.caption: Sir David Bell led the independent review of antisemitism in schools.

sources.originalTitle: Schools in England must recognise antisemitism as distinct category of harm, report says

segments.body: A review led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell says schools and colleges in England should recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it. The government is expected to accept its 27 recommendations, but the report is due to be presented to MPs on Wednesday.

segments.title: Reporting and response
segments.body: Recommendations include dedicated teacher training, resources, a national advice hotline and robust systems for reporting incidents. A survey for the review found that three in five Jewish students said they had experienced antisemitism; fewer than half of students surveyed thought reported cases would be addressed.

perspectives.body: The Board of Deputies of British Jews says treating antisemitism as a safeguarding issue could make schools explicitly responsible for addressing it and strengthen accountability.

content.headline: Russell Brand accuser tells court he continued after she asked him to stop
content.shortHeadline: Accuser tells court Brand continued after she asked him to stop
content.standfirst: A woman’s recorded police interview was played at the comedian’s trial, where he denies three rape charges and other alleged sexual offences. The proceedings continue.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hears

segments.body: A woman told police that Russell Brand raped her at his London home in 2009 and continued after she asked him to stop, the court heard as her recorded interview was played. She said he later told her to “clear up the mess you’ve made”. Brand denies three rape charges, three sexual assault charges and one indecent assault charge involving six women.

segments.title: Other evidence heard
segments.body: Two other women gave evidence from behind a screen on Tuesday, each alleging sexual assault at work. One said Brand squeezed her breasts and kissed her; the other said he put his head in her lap during a filming project. These are allegations being heard in court, not findings of guilt.

content.headline: England plans tighter rules on high-risk non-surgical cosmetic procedures
content.shortHeadline: England plans tighter rules for high-risk cosmetic procedures
content.standfirst: Government proposals would restrict who can perform treatments such as liquid BBLs and chemical peels, ban high-risk procedures for under-18s and introduce fines. The rules are planned for 2027 and remain subject to consultation.

sources.originalTitle: Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong

segments.body: The government plans to limit high-risk non-surgical cosmetic procedures in England to properly trained professionals. The proposed rules would also ban such treatments for under-18s and create new offences and fines of up to £4,000 for providers who break the law. The government will consult before draft rules go to Parliament in spring 2027.

segments.title: Calls for broader safeguards
segments.body: The plans follow reports of dangerous procedures carried out in homes and other unsuitable settings, as well as serious injuries and deaths. The Royal College of Surgeons of England welcomed the proposals but said they did not go far enough, warning that cosmetic surgery itself also needs robust regulation.

perspectives.body: The Royal College of Surgeons says the proposed rules must not create a gap in protection by regulating non-surgical procedures more strongly than cosmetic surgery.

content.headline: New private parking code gives drivers grace periods and appeal rights
content.shortHeadline: New parking code sets grace periods and appeal rights
content.standfirst: Drivers will get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after paid time expires under rules taking effect in December. They will still need to appeal a ticket they believe is unfair.

image.caption: A car park, where the new code will set rules for private parking charges.

sources.originalTitle: The 10-minute parking rule that will see fines waived for drivers

segments.body: A new government code for private car parks sets a five-minute period for drivers to read the signs and decide whether to stay, and 10 minutes to leave after paid time expires. Charges must also be cancelled for specified problems outside a driver’s control, such as a breakdown or a faulty ticket machine.

segments.title: Drivers will need to challenge tickets
segments.body: The code takes effect on 21 December. Drivers who believe a charge is unfair will have to appeal to the parking company, then may take it to a new independent service. Companies that fail to follow the rules could lose access to the DVLA database used to identify vehicle owners. The AA called the changes a good first step but said debt-collection fees remain a concern.

perspectives.body: The AA says the code does not resolve complaints about debt-recovery fees, which can add up to £70 to an unpaid charge.

content.headline: Two men held for three days after alleged espionage at Danish defence firm
content.shortHeadline: Two men held after alleged spying at Danish defence firm
content.standfirst: A judge allowed police to keep the 18- and 21-year-old suspects in custody for three days, but did not order pre-trial detention. Both deny the charges; the court hearing was closed.

image.caption: MyDefence, based in Nørresundby, makes equipment to detect and counter drones.

sources.originalTitle: Efter timelangt grundlovsforhør må politiet holde på sigtede i spionagesag i tre døgn
To mænd er sigtet for spionage mod dansk forsvarsvirksomhed - her er, hvad vi ved

segments.body: Two Ukrainian men, aged 18 and 21, may be held for three days after a closed hearing in Aalborg. They are suspected of photographing defence company MyDefence in Nørresundby on 19 October and sending images to someone on Telegram. Both deny the espionage charges. Their lawyer says the younger man was shaken by the accusation.

segments.title: Key details remain unknown
segments.body: Prosecutors allege that a Russian intelligence service is involved, but have not identified which one. The suspects’ account and the purpose of the photographs have not been made public because the hearing was held behind closed doors. MyDefence has declined to comment.

perspectives.body: DR’s explainer says PET is assisting the investigation and has warned generally that people recruited online to photograph defence companies or other sensitive sites could be helping with espionage or sabotage.

content.headline: Danish report links severe stress to lost work and long-term disability
content.shortHeadline: Danish report links severe stress to long-term work loss
content.standfirst: The Economic Councils estimate that severe stress has reduced the labour force by 99,000 people and contributed to 91,000 early-retirement cases. A separate account follows one woman’s lengthy struggle to return to work.

image.caption: Julia Hinderberger uses notes to help her remember after years of illness following a stress reaction.

sources.originalTitle: Stress sender titusindvis uden for arbejdsmarkedet, viser ny rapport
Hun kom til Danmark som højtuddannet arbejdskraft - men er endt på førtidspension

segments.body: A report by Denmark’s Economic Councils estimates that severe stress has reduced the country’s labour supply by 99,000 people, with up to 39,000 cases assessed as work-related. It also says 91,000 people have ended up on early-retirement pensions after severe stress. The report links the issue to both individual hardship and public finances.

segments.title: Recovery can take years
segments.body: The report says one in 10 people affected by a stress reaction are not back in work 12 years later. DR’s account of Julia Hinderberger describes a long illness after a work-related stress reaction in 2017, repeated attempts to return to employment and her eventual award of an early-retirement pension this year.

perspectives.body: The Danish Employers’ Confederation says stress may arise from private circumstances as well as work, while the Economic Council and the Economic Council of the Labour Movement argue that better working environments can help people remain in employment.

content.headline: More than half of Denmark’s 21-year-olds now live with their parents
content.shortHeadline: More than half of Danish 21-year-olds live at home
content.standfirst: The share living with parents rose from 32% in 2011 to 57% in 2025. Researchers point to housing costs, distance to education and the appeal of having space at home.

image.caption: A growing share of 21-year-olds in Denmark live with their parents.

sources.originalTitle: Flere end hver anden 21-årig bor stadig hos forældre

segments.body: The proportion of 21-year-olds living with their parents rose from 32% in 2011 to 57% in 2025, according to Statistics Denmark figures cited in a new Realdania study. The share varies widely by location: it is 61% in Albertslund and 14% on Læsø.

segments.title: Several factors may explain the rise
segments.body: Realdania points to high housing prices and young people’s satisfaction with living at home. Researchers also cite distance to education, cultural differences and the size of family homes, which can offer young adults more privacy than a small, expensive room elsewhere. The study found no overall difference in quality of life between young people living at home and those who had moved out.

content.headline: Animal group says nearly two-thirds of Salling’s chicken sales are fast-growing
content.shortHeadline: Animal group says fast-growing chickens dominate Salling sales
content.standfirst: Anima says nearly two-thirds of chickens sold by Salling Group are fast-growing breeds, despite a pledge to phase them out. The retailer says supply and demand have slowed the transition.

image.caption: Fast-growing chickens remain the best-selling type at Netto, Føtex and Bilka, according to Anima.

sources.originalTitle: Salling lovede at udfase turbokyllinger - det har de ikke gjort

segments.body: Animal-welfare organisation Anima says nearly two-thirds of chicken sold at Bilka, Føtex and Netto is fast-growing. It says Salling Group has not fulfilled a pledge to phase out the birds, which the company made in 2023. Salling is Denmark’s largest grocery group.

segments.title: Retailer cites supply and demand
segments.body: Salling Group says it still intends to phase out fast-growing chickens but faces limited supply and insufficient demand for higher-welfare alternatives. Anima disputes that explanation, saying producers would switch if the retailer placed orders and committed to buying the birds.

perspectives.body: Salling Group says customers are increasingly choosing cheaper options and that sales of higher-welfare chicken have nevertheless increased.

content.headline: Danish government has yet to say who qualifies for extra pension payment
content.shortHeadline: Who qualifies for Denmark’s extra pension payment remains unclear
content.standfirst: The government says 150,000 pensioners with the lowest means may receive an extra 1,000 kroner a month, but has not set out the eligibility criteria. The delay is drawing criticism from advocacy groups and opposition politicians.

sources.originalTitle: 1.000 kroner ekstra om måneden? 'Regeringen holder de danske pensionister lidt for nar'

segments.body: Five months after the government announced plans for extra support, it has not explained which 150,000 pensioners would receive 1,000 kroner a month. Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard says the criteria are being discussed with parties that may support the measure, which is expected to cost more than two billion kroner.

segments.title: Disagreement over who should benefit
segments.body: The pensioners’ organisation Ældre Sagen says the delay undermines financial security and argues that fixed eligibility cut-offs could treat people unfairly. The Danish People’s Party says the government is misleading pensioners, while the government says it intends to help those with the least. Enhedslisten says a separate agreement could provide clarity sooner.

perspectives.body: The pensioners’ organisation would prefer all 1.1 million state pensioners to receive the payment, while the government says the support is intended for those with the least.

content.headline: Denmark proposes criminal penalties for paying politicians to give up seats
content.shortHeadline: Denmark proposes ban on buying elected seats
content.standfirst: A bill would make it an offence to offer money to a politician to resign or decline a seat, punishable by a fine or up to two years in prison. It follows a 2023 offer by Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s party to an MP.

image.caption: A recording revealed the offer made by Lars Løkke Rasmussen and the Moderates to Mike Fonseca.

sources.originalTitle: Efter Løkkes kælder-tilbud til Fonseca: Nyt lovforslag skal stoppe køb af mandater

segments.body: A draft bill would make it illegal to offer or receive financial benefits in exchange for leaving, or not taking up, an elected post. The proposed penalty is a fine or up to two years in prison. The Folketing’s Rules of Procedure Committee is due to discuss the bill on Wednesday.

segments.title: A response to a previous offer
segments.body: The proposal follows a 2023 incident in which Lars Løkke Rasmussen, on behalf of the Moderates, offered then-MP Mike Fonseca 370,000 kroner to leave parliament so a party substitute could take his seat. The bill says existing law did not prohibit the offer, prompting work on clearer rules.

content.headline: Four Danish opposition parties demand tax cuts for lower-paid workers
content.shortHeadline: Four opposition parties demand broader Danish tax cuts
content.standfirst: Venstre, Liberal Alliance, the Conservatives and the Denmark Democrats say workers earning below 58,000 kroner a month should also receive tax relief. They say they will not support the government’s plan otherwise.

sources.originalTitle: Fire blå partier vil have skattelettelser til alle i regeringens plan

segments.body: Four centre-right parties say the government’s proposed tax plan should include people earning below about 58,000 kroner a month. The government wants to abolish the top-top tax and middle tax, changes that would benefit higher earners, as well as reduce corporation tax by three percentage points from 2030.

segments.title: Support may be needed
segments.body: The four parties say they will not vote for the plan without tax cuts for people on lower and ordinary wages. The government may need their support because its usual supporting parties, Enhedslisten and Alternativet, are not expected to back several of the proposals.

content.headline: Danish police commissioner charged over alleged wine-price fraud
content.shortHeadline: Danish police commissioner charged over alleged wine fraud
content.standfirst: A police commissioner is accused of switching expensive wine into cheaper boxes at a border shop on three visits, including once while on duty. He is also charged with misuse of police systems and denies no known position on the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Politikommissær anklaget for kreativ vin-svindel i grænseshop

segments.body: A Danish police commissioner is charged with fraud and abuse of office over three visits to the Fleggaard border shop in 2025, according to an indictment obtained by DR. He allegedly replaced cheaper wine with more expensive bottles and returned the next day to pay the lower price. The claimed saving was 5,080 kroner.

segments.title: Separate allegation over police records
segments.body: The 39-year-old is also accused of making 20 unauthorised searches of police systems, including looking up personal identification numbers and taking a photograph of a person under arrest. One alleged wine trip was made in a police car while he was on duty. The case is due before Sønderborg District Court on Friday; DR says his response to the charges is not known.

content.headline: Ngumoha inspires Liverpool's seven-goal comeback win over Villarreal
content.shortHeadline: Ngumoha sparks Liverpool comeback against Villarreal
content.standfirst: The 18-year-old helped turn a two-goal deficit into a 4-3 Champions League win, setting up two goals and earning the player-of-the-match award. His fearless display also made history for Liverpool.

image.caption: Rio Ngumoha, who became Liverpool's youngest player to score or assist in the Champions League.

sources.originalTitle: The night 'ruthless' Ngumoha came of age for Liverpool

segments.body: Liverpool trailed Villarreal by two goals before Alexis Mac Allister pulled one back. Rio Ngumoha then supplied the cross for Ronald Araujo's equaliser and, after the break, set up Mac Allister to put Liverpool ahead. Florian Wirtz added a fourth in the 4-3 win.

segments.title: A landmark performance
segments.body: At 18 years and 52 days, Ngumoha became the youngest Liverpool player to score or assist for the club in the Champions League. He completed seven of eight dribbles and had 12 touches in the opposition box. Head coach Andoni Iraola praised his attitude, while stressing that the teenager is still developing.

content.headline: Foden scores a hat-trick as Manchester City beat AEK Athens 5-1
content.shortHeadline: Foden's hat-trick leads City's 5-1 Champions League win
content.standfirst: Phil Foden had a hand in four goals as City pulled clear after AEK briefly made it 2-1. His performance offered a timely reminder of his scoring ability and gave Enzo Maresca a look at him in a central role.

image.caption: Phil Foden, who scored a hat-trick and provided an assist against AEK Athens.

sources.originalTitle: No Haaland, no problem - can Foden be Man City's alternative goalscorer?

segments.body: Foden scored three times and assisted another goal in City's 5-1 win over AEK Athens. His second strike was a first-time finish into the top corner. It was his first Premier League goal in 10 months at the weekend, followed by a Champions League hat-trick that he said was good for his confidence.

segments.title: A possible option up front
segments.body: Erling Haaland was named in the squad but rested after taking a blow to his foot in the previous game. Foden started on the right before moving into a false-nine role, which he said he enjoyed. Manager Enzo Maresca said he considers Foden one of England's best players and expects him to help the team.

content.headline: Pakistan's Arafat Minhas takes six as England collapse in ODI opener
content.shortHeadline: Arafat's six wickets send England to defeat by Pakistan
content.standfirst: England were bowled out for 215 chasing Pakistan's 302-9, losing their last seven wickets for 50 runs. Arafat Minhas made 59 and took 6-40 as England began their winter with a heavy defeat.

image.caption: Pakistan's Arafat Minhas, who made 59 and took 6-40 against England.

sources.originalTitle: Sloppy England start winter with Pakistan defeat

segments.body: Arafat Minhas made 59 after being dropped on 12, helping Pakistan reach 302-9. He then took six wickets as England's chase fell apart: after a 91-run opening stand, England lost seven wickets for 50 and finished on 215. Tom Banton top-scored for England with 57.

segments.title: A test for England's World Cup build-up
segments.body: England captain Harry Brook said his side had expected to chase the target but lost too many wickets in clumps and needed to put the spinners under more pressure. This was the first of a potential 21 ODIs before next year's World Cup; England were also without Jos Buttler, Jofra Archer and Jacob Bethell.

content.headline: Mark Allen considers retirement after Northern Ireland Open defeat
content.shortHeadline: Allen says retirement is on his mind after Belfast exit
content.standfirst: The former world number one lost 4-2 to Jordan Brown on his return to competition and said retirement is something he has been considering. Allen has not made a decision, but says something must change before the UK Championship.

image.caption: Mark Allen after his Northern Ireland Open defeat, as he considers his future in snooker.

sources.originalTitle: Allen considers retirement after NI Open exit

segments.body: Allen said simply “Yeah” when asked if he was considering retirement after losing 4-2 to fellow Antrim player Jordan Brown in the Northern Ireland Open first round. He said playing the match was an achievement after a difficult period and that he had wanted his last match, if it came to that, to be in Belfast.

segments.title: No decision yet
segments.body: Allen said he would not announce retirement immediately after a defeat, but that something needed to change within six weeks for him to return for the UK Championship. The 40-year-old has won 12 ranking tournaments. Brown said he hoped Allen would continue, while acknowledging his own difficult circumstances.

content.headline: Swiatek ends her season after thigh injury and misses WTA Finals
content.shortHeadline: Swiatek ends a difficult season early
content.standfirst: The six-time Grand Slam champion has withdrawn from Ningbo with a thigh injury and will not qualify for the WTA Finals. She says she needs a longer period to rest and recover before returning in 2027.

image.caption: Iga Swiatek, whose 2026 season ends after a thigh injury.

sources.originalTitle: Swiatek ends 'most demanding' season of career

segments.body: Iga Swiatek has ended her 2026 season after withdrawing from the Ningbo Open with a thigh injury. The world number nine will miss the WTA Finals for the first time since 2019. She said the past few months, and years, had been intense and that she needed to recover fully.

segments.title: A season of change
segments.body: Swiatek ends the year with one title, the Canadian Open, and a 42-16 win-loss record. She did not reach a Grand Slam quarter-final in 2026, and her latest major title was Wimbledon last year. After changing coaches in March, she said she was proud of her work and progress in the second half of the season.

content.headline: Bavuma's 179 gives South Africa a chance to fight back against Australia
content.shortHeadline: Bavuma's 179 revives South Africa against Australia
content.standfirst: Temba Bavuma batted through South Africa's recovery from 110-6 to make his highest Test score and help his side declare. Kagiso Rabada then struck in Australia's reply, leaving the hosts with a chance to revive the series.

image.caption: Temba Bavuma, whose 179 was his highest Test score.

sources.originalTitle: Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia?

segments.body: South Africa captain Temba Bavuma made 179, his highest Test score, after arriving at the crease with his side 12-2 on day one. He shared a 183-run eighth-wicket partnership with Simon Harmer and helped South Africa recover from 110-6 before declaring on 425-9.

segments.title: A chance, but no result yet
segments.body: Rabada dismissed Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of the reply, but poor light soon stopped play. Bavuma said the innings had given South Africa a chance, while acknowledging that an earlier declaration might have allowed more overs in favourable conditions. The Test was still in progress in the report.

content.headline: Champions League goals record raises questions about entertainment and jeopardy
content.shortHeadline: Champions League goals surge sets a new record
content.standfirst: This season's competition is averaging 4.16 goals a game, its highest rate in Champions League history. The scoring surge is drawing praise for the entertainment, as well as questions about what the expanded format means for jeopardy.

image.caption: Phil Foden, who scored a hat-trick in Manchester City's 5-1 win over AEK Athens.

sources.originalTitle: No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record

segments.body: The Champions League has produced 187 goals at an average of 4.16 per game, the highest rate in its history. Forty goals were scored across Tuesday's nine matches. Last week's two matchdays produced 78 goals, the highest-scoring matchday total since the league phase began.

segments.title: More goals, but what do they mean?
segments.body: The 36-team league phase replaced groups of four with eight matches for each side. Some argue that the format gives teams room to play more expansively because a defeat early on is less costly. Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live that the games are thrilling, but questioned whether the reduced jeopardy makes the results feel less meaningful.

content.headline: Jake Smith's story highlights the risks of under-fuelling in sport
content.shortHeadline: Runner Jake Smith explains the danger of REDs
content.standfirst: British runner Jake Smith says he was diagnosed with relative energy deficiency in sport after repeated injuries and under-fuelling. Experts and athletes explain how REDs can affect men as well as women, and why it may go unnoticed.

sources.originalTitle: Race, illness, injury, repeat - REDs and why men are suffering in silence

segments.body: Jake Smith says he suffered two stress fractures in four months before being diagnosed with relative energy deficiency in sport, or REDs. The condition can result from insufficient energy intake and may cause injuries, fatigue, disrupted sleep and longer-term health problems if left untreated.

segments.title: Why it can be missed
segments.body: The report says REDs can be harder to recognise in men, where symptoms such as falling testosterone and fatigue may be less obvious. Triathlete Jonny Brownlee described under-fuelling as a contributor to injuries in his career; experts say the condition is reversible, but warn that athletes may mistake it for burnout or fail to match their food intake to training demands.

content.headline: Kiran Leonard finds a path beyond the teenage-prodigy label
content.shortHeadline: Kiran Leonard moves beyond the prodigy years
content.standfirst: Once patronised for his precocious, densely composed music, the Saddleworth-born artist describes leaving his first industry team and finding a new creative community in London.

image.caption: Kiran Leonard, experimental musician and songwriter.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy

segments.body: Kiran Leonard was hailed as a prodigy at 16, but says early coverage fetishised the ambition and complexity of his music in ways that felt patronising. After releasing four albums, he ditched his management team without a plan and struggled to find gigs or a new manager.

segments.title: Finding a different voice
segments.body: Leonard gradually found his footing through shows and friendships with musicians including Caroline. He now sees his work as a series of distinct investigations, and says he is drawn less to stylistic labels than to sounds that create a physical feeling. Much of his work remains solitary, with collaborations offering a different voice.

content.headline: Brazilian pop fandoms mobilise online for Lula ahead of the runoff
content.shortHeadline: Brazilian pop fans campaign for Lula
content.standfirst: More than 600 fan groups have joined a digital campaign backing Brazil’s president in the 25 October runoff. Their organisers see fan communities as a way to bring political debate to people who may not follow it elsewhere.

image.caption: Two pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?

segments.body: After the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, more than 600 fan groups for international and Brazilian pop artists joined Fandoms Pelo Brasil, an online campaign supporting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro is scheduled for 25 October. The campaign grew from fan accounts offering Lula’s team access to their social media audiences.

perspectives.body: Organisers say fan accounts can carry political discussion to people who follow artists and fan communities but do not keep up with politics. The reporting also notes the limits: some Brazilian fan groups back Bolsonaro, while Shakira’s team has restricted political use of her image.

segments.title: Fandom becomes a campaign network
segments.body: The effort has moved from online posts to street organising, with pop-culture symbols appearing at a Lula rally in São Paulo. The government has also courted fans through measures such as a decree targeting ticket-scalping bots and requiring free drinking water at large public events. The groups’ support is not presented as universal, but their mobilisation has become part of the runoff campaign.

content.headline: Ed Sanders reflects on the Fugs and a life of countercultural protest
content.shortHeadline: Ed Sanders on the Fugs and a life of protest
content.standfirst: The 87-year-old musician, poet and activist speaks as a documentary about the Fugs reaches UK audiences, revisiting the band’s anti-war theatrics, battles over censorship and eclectic music.

image.caption: Ed Sanders, right, with Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture

segments.body: Ed Sanders led the Fugs, whose mix of poetry, folk, garage rock and theatrical provocation made them part of New York’s 1960s counterculture. Speaking as the documentary Fugs Film! receives its UK premiere, Sanders recalls the band’s aim to protest the American war machine as well as make music.

perspectives.body: Sanders says the group’s plan to “levitate” the Pentagon was a deliberately absurd spectacle designed to focus attention on an anti-war protest. He describes that activism as a continuing struggle, not a victory secured in the 1960s.

segments.title: Art, provocation and the cost of refusing to compromise
segments.body: The band’s provocations brought censorship battles and, Sanders says, helped cost them an Atlantic Records release after he refused to remove an offensive song. He now sees some of the group’s songs differently, but argues that music and protest belonged together in the Fugs’ work.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn advertising jingles into a bittersweet sound collage
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches make a collage of commercial noise
content.standfirst: No Bad Memories folds advertising voices and audio logos into the Australian group’s sample-rich pop. The review hears an exuberant, sprawling record shadowed by the fading shared references of mass media.

sources.originalTitle: No Bad Memories

segments.body: On No Bad Memories, the Avalanches build a continuous, 52-minute collage from decades of advertising jingles, audio logos and spoken copy, alongside vintage soul and easy listening. The interruption of a dance track by a flatly delivered “Toshiba” is both a joke and a reminder that the record’s playful sound is not outside commercial culture.

segments.title: A nostalgia without a monoculture
segments.body: The review finds the album closer to the immersive sample collage of Since I Left You than the group’s more conventional later songwriting, while noting its long track list and numerous interludes. Its deeper melancholy comes from the question of whether a sound can still summon collective nostalgia when audiences no longer share the same mass-media touchstones.

content.headline: Zach Bryan’s new EP finds focus in sobriety and a bid for adulthood
content.shortHeadline: Zach Bryan finds focus on a new EP
content.standfirst: On Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs, the country songwriter pares back his usual sprawl to examine sobriety, love and the damage of old habits. The review sees a more controlled, forward-looking record.

sources.originalTitle: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs EP

segments.body: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs is Zach Bryan’s first music written and recorded while sober. Across eight songs, he looks back at personal turmoil and the habits he is trying to leave behind, in a more concise and controlled set than his often sprawling albums.

segments.title: The unevenness of moving on
segments.body: The review hears his strongest writing in songs about change, including a duet with Turnpike Troubadours singer Evan Felker that links shared roots to the difficult work of breaking harmful habits. A duet with Lana Del Rey is judged less successful, but the record’s overall movement from recent mistakes towards a possible future gives it its shape.

content.headline: Way Dynamic’s Massive Shoe finds tenderness in bruised pop songs
content.shortHeadline: Way Dynamic make warm pop with a bruised edge
content.standfirst: Dylan Young’s Melbourne group draws on familiar pop sounds for gentle melodies, but the album’s strongest moments turn on rambling guitars and sharply expressed regret.

sources.originalTitle: Massive Shoe

segments.body: Way Dynamic’s third album, Massive Shoe, moves between bright, guitar-led pop and looser, more searching songs. The review hears the record’s warmth in its stacked harmonies and melodic ease, but finds its most affecting work where that lightness meets the sting of a failed relationship.

segments.title: When the regret cuts through
segments.body: “Miffed It” is singled out for its plain admission of a love mishandled, while “I Was the Dancer” opens into an unexpectedly expansive, jam-like passage. Some of the album’s more playful references and arrangements are less substantial, but the review values the tension between Young’s sunny musical surfaces and unsettled lyrics.

content.headline: Renny Conti’s Split Second renders grief as a shifting haze
content.shortHeadline: Renny Conti writes through grief’s haze
content.standfirst: Written after the death of his older brother, Split Second moves between soft, drifting arrangements and moments of startling clarity. The review finds its most powerful passages when Conti’s memories become sharply specific.

sources.originalTitle: Split Second

segments.body: Renny Conti wrote Split Second in the months after his older brother Andrew died. Its quiet voice and slow-moving arrangements evoke grief as a disorienting presence: the knowledge that someone is gone colliding with the feeling that they remain close.

segments.title: Moments that come into focus
segments.body: The review praises the album’s hazy atmosphere but sometimes longs for more detail to break through it. A direct line placing Conti in Prospect Park as he writes to escape a “death-induced funk” provides that clarity; the album is most affecting, the critic argues, when its private loss takes vivid, particular form.

content.headline: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea turns indie pop into a playful musical
content.shortHeadline: Worldpeace DMT make a playful indie-pop musical
content.standfirst: The London duo’s digitally assembled songs sound like a deliberately scrappy stage show, balancing schoolyard playfulness with moments of genuine ache. The review finds the apparent silliness more carefully made than it first appears.

sources.originalTitle: Stick Around for Tea

segments.body: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea pares back the sound collage of the duo’s debut in favour of songs that feel like scenes in a low-budget musical. Chiptuned textures, toy-like sounds and singsong vocals keep the record playful, while Rowan Please’s performance and Leo Fincham’s arrangements reveal a deliberate tension between childhood and adulthood.

segments.title: A joke with feeling underneath
segments.body: The review points to “Stratocaster” as a sparse, darkly poetic song delivered with the simplicity of a nursery rhyme, and to the title track’s engineered contrast between synthetic rhythm and a human chorus. The record repeatedly invites the question of whether its creators are serious; the critic’s answer is that the self-conscious play is part of the craft, not evidence against it.

content.headline: Michael Jackson biopic sequel may address abuse allegations from his perspective
content.shortHeadline: Michael Jackson sequel may address abuse allegations
content.standfirst: Jaafar Jackson says a second film will offer more of his uncle’s point of view. That approach follows criticism that the authorised first biopic omitted allegations and the perspectives of those who made them.

image.caption: Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in the film Michael.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s important that Michael’s voice is heard’: Jaafar Jackson says second biopic of his uncle will cover sexual abuse allegations

segments.body: Jaafar Jackson, who made his screen debut playing his uncle in Michael, says a second film will give more attention to the late singer’s perspective on the sexual abuse allegations against him. The first biopic did not address the allegations; a legal clause prevented the depiction of one accuser, and a planned police-raid sequence was cut.

segments.title: A disputed account
segments.body: Jackson says the family has wanted the singer’s voice heard. Dan Reed, director of the documentary Leaving Neverland, sharply criticised the first film for distorting the subject and excluding the allegations. Jackson was accused of sexually abusing a child in 1993 and settled out of court; he was acquitted of other child sexual abuse charges in 2005. How a sequel will handle the competing accounts remains unknown.

perspectives.body: Reed says the first biopic reversed the truth by presenting Jackson without serious scrutiny and objected to its omission of the allegations. Jaafar Jackson, by contrast, says a sequel should give greater weight to his uncle’s point of view.

content.headline: Ghosts cast explain why the finished sitcom is returning as a film
content.shortHeadline: Why the Ghosts team brought the story back as a film
content.standfirst: The creators say they had no plan to revive their sitcom after its 2023 finale. A new film gave them a way to reunite the ensemble without simply stretching a television episode to feature length.

image.caption: The Ghosts cast in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff

segments.body: Ghosts ended in 2023 with its creators believing the story was complete. The cast says a film only became appealing after they found a premise—possession—that could let one of the ghosts leave Button House and create stakes suited to a feature. The result, Ghosts: The Possession of Button House, continues the story without restarting the series.

segments.title: A reunion, not a promise of more
segments.body: The team describes the production as a quick decision driven partly by missing one another after years of working together. They are cautious about promising further films, though Laurence Rickard jokes that caveman Robin could support a spin-off. The creators say there is no secret project in development.

content.headline: Sitges festival finds horror in motherhood, politics and the uncanny
content.shortHeadline: The unsettling discoveries of the Sitges film festival
content.standfirst: This year’s fantastic film festival ranged from sinister children and body horror to an Indonesian prison ghost story. The critic’s highlights include films that mix genre shocks with social unease and unexpected warmth.

image.caption: A scene from The Spiral, one of the films screened at Sitges.

sources.originalTitle: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory

segments.body: The 59th Sitges festival was crowded with stories of fraught motherhood, from Nightborn’s unsettling newborn to films about postpartum depression and a child who disrupts a scout troop. Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine won best feature, while the festival also recognised performances in The Spiral and The Birthday Party.

segments.title: Standout films beyond the competition
segments.body: The critic’s favourites included a time-loop story that darkens as it unfolds, a return to J-horror in The Mouths, and Sabu’s crime comedy Arrested Memory. The strongest recommendation is Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, which layers a supernatural curse onto prison violence and a critique of Indonesian corruption while retaining an unexpectedly warmhearted tone.

content.headline: Children of the Wicker Man turns a folk-horror legacy into family history
content.shortHeadline: The family story behind The Wicker Man
content.standfirst: Robin Hardy’s sons revisit the making and afterlife of his cult film, but the documentary’s personal force comes with gaps in the family account and unanswered questions about absent voices.

image.caption: A still from Children of the Wicker Man.

sources.originalTitle: Children of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made it

segments.body: Children of the Wicker Man, made by Robin Hardy’s sons Justin and Dominic, connects the troubled production of the 1973 film with its rise from box-office failure to cult status. It also becomes a personal reckoning with a father who left one son’s life, making the documentary’s family history as prominent as the film’s legacy.

segments.title: The silences in the account
segments.body: The review admires the brothers’ willingness to share painful memories but finds the film weakened by missing perspectives, including those of their siblings and other people central to the story. Justin’s anger and Dominic’s greater sympathy give the documentary distinct emotional registers, but do not resolve the absences.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office failure sharpens its bleak climate-change warning
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s flop sharpens its climate warning
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise’s misanthropic satire has been pulled from many US cinemas after a disastrous opening. The film’s critic argues that its depiction of public complicity makes it a revealing, if deeply flawed, climate story.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time

segments.body: In Digger, an oilman’s drilling triggers a vast iceberg that threatens Europe. The film has been savaged by critics and suffered a steep box-office drop; the article reports a predicted loss of $245m and says it was removed from more than 2,500 US theatres before its third week.

segments.title: A critique with its own blind spots
segments.body: The argument for the film is that it goes beyond blaming one oil executive, confronting viewers with their own dependence on fossil fuels and the reluctance to change. But the piece also notes its nihilism and its dismissal of clean energy, which undercuts the urgency of that critique. Its failure may also make studios less willing to back similarly direct climate films.

content.headline: Judi Dench calls Cats a waste of goodwill and talent
content.shortHeadline: Judi Dench reflects on the failed Cats film
content.standfirst: In a forthcoming memoir, Dench says the film’s intentions were honourable but its elements did not come together. She also describes discomfort on set and recalls the hostile response to the finished adaptation.

image.caption: Judi Dench as Old Deuteronomy in Cats.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’

segments.body: Judi Dench writes in her forthcoming memoir that the 2019 film adaptation of Cats was “a waste of all that goodwill and talent”. She says she never saw the final cut and cannot judge it herself, but understands why critics were hostile and felt ill at ease in her role as Old Deuteronomy.

segments.title: An unsuccessful production without villains
segments.body: Dench criticises how young dancers were left exhausted and ignored between takes, while also saying nobody set out to make a bad film and that the people involved had honourable intentions. Andrew Lloyd Webber has been much harsher, calling the adaptation wrong and saying the experience left him emotionally damaged.

perspectives.body: Dench describes a failed collaboration without assigning blame to individual makers. Lloyd Webber, who was not consulted in the way he expected, has repeatedly condemned the film and its treatment of the original musical.

content.headline: Hartlepool fishers turn suspected pollution into an environmental campaign
content.shortHeadline: Hartlepool fishers take their pollution concerns to film
content.standfirst: Jeanie Finlay’s documentary follows fishermen facing collapsing catches after a mass marine die-off. Their independent study finds evidence of a possible link to industrial chemicals, while officials have disputed their account.

image.caption: Hartlepool fisherman Stan Rennie in All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.

sources.originalTitle: All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activism

segments.body: After thousands of crabs, starfish and lobsters washed up dead on the northeast coast in 2021, Hartlepool fishermen suspected industrial pollution. An official investigation pointed instead to an algal bloom; unconvinced, the fishermen funded an independent study, which found evidence of a link to pyridine, a byproduct of steelmaking.

perspectives.body: The documentary follows the fishermen’s investigation and their belief that sediment dredged from the River Tees and dumped at sea may be responsible. The review reports evidence of a possible chemical link, not a settled finding of causation.

segments.title: Livelihoods and local power
segments.body: With catches down 80%, rising fuel costs and boats up for sale, the fishermen’s campaign is also a fight for their livelihoods. The film links the dispute to dredging for a Tees Valley freeport and shows the mayor dismissing the fishermen as conspiracy theorists and activists.

content.headline: Smart TVs leave some viewers worried about privacy and control
content.shortHeadline: Viewers push back against smart TV surveillance
content.standfirst: Some owners are disconnecting devices, modifying remotes or buying simpler screens to avoid unwanted updates, adverts and data collection. A report alleging LG TVs record audio has been denied by the company.

image.caption: A viewer with a smart television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV

segments.body: Some viewers say smart TVs have become harder to use as software updates, paid-service prompts and advertising crowd out the simple functions they want. Several people interviewed keep their screens offline or use external devices, citing both reliability and privacy concerns.

perspectives.body: TV specialist Tom Parsons says cheaper sets can slow under the demands of their software, while noting that most shoppers still want an all-in-one entertainment system. That preference has left few straightforward, non-connected televisions on sale.

segments.title: The limits of opting out
segments.body: The article describes a YouTube investigation alleging that LG televisions record audio even when offline or powered down; LG denied the allegations. Some owners have responded by modifying devices, while proposed changes to broadcast services in the UK and Australia could make internet-connected viewing harder to avoid.

content.headline: Freddie Meredith goes from bar work to SNL UK in a rapid comedy ascent
content.shortHeadline: Freddie Meredith’s unlikely leap to SNL UK
content.standfirst: After waiting tables and reworking a struggling Edinburgh show, the comedian was asked to join Saturday Night Live UK at short notice. He discusses the awkward characters and observations that helped him find an audience.

image.caption: Comedian and SNL UK cast member Freddie Meredith.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leagues

segments.body: Freddie Meredith was working in a bar and preparing for his Edinburgh Fringe debut when his character show Need a Light? began to find an audience. A best newcomer nomination and a sold-out London transfer followed; just before the final Fringe performance, he was invited to join the cast of Saturday Night Live UK.

segments.title: The comedy of uncomfortable men
segments.body: Meredith’s work focuses on socially awkward men trying to fit in, drawing on jobs behind bars and small observations of people at the edge of a scene. He says his interest in men drawn to misogynistic online ideas is both comic material and a subject that needs careful handling: audiences may laugh without recognising the behaviour as troubling.

content.headline: Linda Cardellini embraces practical gore in Friday the 13th prequel
content.shortHeadline: Linda Cardellini enters the world of slasher horror
content.standfirst: In Crystal Lake, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original Friday the 13th killer. She describes the hands-on prosthetics behind the show’s bloodiest scenes and reflects on the long afterlife of Freaks and Geeks.

image.caption: Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake

segments.body: Linda Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake, a prequel to the Friday the 13th films. She says one of the show’s most gruesome effects—a face pulled off with fishing wire—was created with practical prosthetics, and that seeing it happen helped shape her reaction.

segments.title: A career of unexpected turns
segments.body: Cardellini also looks back on Freaks and Geeks, cancelled before its first season had finished airing but later embraced as a lasting television favourite. After winning her first Emmy for DTF St Louis, she says she enjoys changing direction rather than committing to a “scream queen” identity.

content.headline: Aberfan survivors recall the long fight for justice in new documentary
content.shortHeadline: Aberfan’s families and their decades-long fight
content.standfirst: The documentary revisits the 1966 disaster and the failures that followed it, through the memories of survivors and bereaved families. Its review finds the treatment of the village by officials as distressing as the tragedy itself.

image.caption: The aftermath of the Aberfan disaster in 1966.

sources.originalTitle: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening

segments.body: On 21 October 1966, a spoil tip engulfed a school and homes in Aberfan, killing 116 children and 28 adults. Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back begins with survivors’ and families’ memories before tracing the campaign to hold the National Coal Board and government to account.

segments.title: A second injury
segments.body: The documentary recounts how the inquiry blamed the Coal Board, yet no one was personally punished. Families also faced years of resistance over liability and the removal of the tips; the board demanded money from the disaster fund to pay for the work. The review highlights the village’s organising and the later return of the fund money by the Blair government.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from The Audacity to Lupin
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: A new comedy about wealthy tech executives leads this week’s picks, alongside a killer-gnome series, a grooming documentary and new seasons of familiar streaming favourites.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Audacity, from Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, sends up a rich, morally compromised tech CEO and the world around him. The guide says the comedy does not quite reach Succession’s heights, but finds plenty of bite in its portrait of people insulated by wealth.

segments.title: Other picks this week
segments.body: The week’s recommendations range from Australian horror-comedy Gnomes and a documentary about the online grooming and murder of Breck Bednar to returning series Nobody Wants This and Lupin. The selection also includes a Halloween edition of Last One Laughing and a three-part investigation into police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: a ketamine documentary and rare Only Fools and Horses clips
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: ketamine, Only Fools and more
content.standfirst: Stacey Dooley meets long-term ketamine users, while Only Fools and Horses fans get a look at deleted scenes. The evening’s other picks include a family documentary and a Bafta-nominated film about addiction.

image.caption: Stacey Dooley in Down the K-Hole.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Stacey Dooley learns about ‘ket bladder’

segments.body: Down the K-Hole follows Stacey Dooley as she speaks with long-term ketamine users about the effects of the drug, including bladder damage and the appeal of dissociation. The programme is presented as an eye-opening account of consequences, not as a first-hand investigation by Dooley into her own use.

segments.title: Other evening choices
segments.body: The schedule also offers previously unseen Only Fools and Horses clips, a documentary about a mother and daughter navigating addiction and estrangement, and a programme about novelist John le Carré. The guide rounds out its picks with baking, police drama and live sport.

content.headline: Time’s young offender institute drama shows how anger is reinforced
content.shortHeadline: Time examines anger inside a young offenders’ institute
content.standfirst: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama follows boys held in near-isolation and the adults responsible for them. Its review finds a devastating account of violence, emotional need and a system that leaves little room for change.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence

segments.body: The final series of Time moves into a young offender institution where boys can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day under a “keep apart” system. David Tennant plays a weary but not entirely unfeeling officer; Siobhan Finneran returns as a chaplain who has lost her faith but continues to work with the inmates.

perspectives.body: The review argues the series should receive the national attention given to Adolescence, while acknowledging that the prison system’s complexity and the bleakness of its subject may make that harder.

segments.title: What the drama makes visible
segments.body: The boys’ histories include serious violence, but the series also shows grief, abuse and a lack of language for emotion feeding further harm. The review praises the young cast and argues that the drama’s account of isolation and pent-up anger makes the realities of young offender institutions difficult to ignore.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party brings class, grief and ambition to television
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel into a drama about a journalist and a Tory politician, and how personal loss and class have shaped her work.

image.caption: Actor, writer and showrunner Sarah Solemani.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: Sarah Solemani stars in and runs The Party, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s novel. The drama follows a working-class journalist and a Conservative politician whose old friendship hides a secret. Solemani says she has long tried to bring stories about the British class system to television without being forced to treat class as a genre in itself.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani speaks about losing her mother at 16, the urgency that followed, and her view that creativity requires a willingness to be emotionally exposed. She also says the #MeToo movement changed working conditions on sets, describing a marked difference from her experience as a young actor.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, critical odyssey
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is a strange Antarctic odyssey
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through a world of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and scattered words. Its fractured storytelling becomes a critique of the human urge to conquer and plunder.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony casts the player as a penguin exploring an Antarctic landscape where Nazis pursue an ancient entity. Words replace the usual treasure as collectibles, and hopping between different penguin species changes how the player moves through the terrain.

segments.title: A history seen from another angle
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling shifts between low-poly exploration, narrated expedition history and archive footage. Its eventual critique of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism is tied to a wider invitation to experience the world without treating it as something to conquer, though technical glitches occasionally interrupt the play.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake makes a classic feel new under the thumbs
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a striking Switch 2 remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake updates movement, camera and sound for Switch 2 while preserving the game’s familiar world and puzzles. Link’s new look is divisive, but the preview finds a coherent reimagining in motion.

image.caption: Link in Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, manual jump, free-rotating camera and a streamlined inventory. Familiar dungeons and puzzles remain, but the upgraded controls make the 1998 game feel markedly different to play.

perspectives.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, wide-eyed redesign as a point of debate, but suggests its doll-like look may reflect a Japanese puppet-theatre tradition rather than a simple pursuit of 4K detail.

segments.title: The challenge of revisiting a classic
segments.body: The remake’s enhanced environments and newly orchestrated soundtrack help refresh the familiar adventure, though the reviewer questions whether Hyrule Field can recreate the freedom players felt in 1998. The more traditional dungeon structure may itself be part of the appeal for returning fans.

content.headline: Could a new wave of independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: Independent arcades could bring gaming back to the high street
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to occupy players indefinitely, interest is growing in shorter experiences and social play. The case for independent arcades is less about nostalgia than shared discovery.

image.caption: Players return to the social experience of arcade gaming.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that publishers’ pursuit of “forever games” has helped renew interest in shorter, more focused experiences. New arcade-minded titles and specialist venues suggest a possible return to gaming spaces where players can try different games without committing all their time to one.

segments.title: A local place for players
